hints: Focus on what actually holds a metal together, the attraction between positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
Both calcium and barium are in Group 2, so each atom provides two delocalised electrons, but the $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ ion is much smaller than the $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ ion.
Connect smaller ionic size to higher charge density and stronger pull on the electrons, so more heat energy is needed to loosen the lattice and melt it.
walkthrough:
**Recall the metallic model**

Both calcium and barium have giant metallic structures. Think of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

Melting breaks the attraction: $\text{M}^{2+} \text{ --- delocalised } e^{-}$

**Compare calcium and barium down Group 2**

Both release 2 electrons per atom, so the charge is the same. The big difference is size.

$$\text{Ca}^{2+} \text{ is smaller than } \text{Ba}^{2+}$$

**Link size to bond strength and melting point**

A smaller ion has the same 2+ charge packed into a smaller volume. That means higher charge density and a stronger pull on the delocalised electrons.

Stronger metallic bonding needs more energy to break, so calcium has the higher melting point.

options.A: Correct. Smaller $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has higher charge density than larger $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, so it attracts the delocalised electrons more strongly. Stronger metallic bonding means a higher melting point.
options.B: Incorrect. Calcium is purely giant metallic, not molecular and not partly covalent. This is a common trap confusing different lattice types.
options.C: Incorrect. Both Group 2 metals contribute 2 delocalised electrons per atom, so the number is the same. Also, ionisation energy decreases down the group, so barium has the lower ionisation energy, not calcium.
options.D: Incorrect. Melting point is controlled by attraction between cations and delocalised electrons, not by repulsion between complete inner shells. More shells simply makes the barium ion larger and the attraction weaker.
